articles.title: Europe to send a diplomat team to Ukraine talks as leaders push for a voice
articles.summary: European Council President Antonio Costa said the continent will be represented by officials from the 27-nation EU bloc and five members of the "Coalition of the Willing" that backs Ukraine: the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Poland.
articles.body: DUBLIN (AP) — Europe will send a team of diplomats from the European Union and five individual countries to the next round of Ukraine talks, a top EU official said Friday after a summit focused on how to avoid being shut out of U.S.-led negotiations on ending the nearly five-year war. European Council President Antonio Costa said the continent will be represented by officials from the 27-nation EU bloc and five members of the "Coalition of the Willing" that backs Ukraine: the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Poland. "We need to integrate all of us. And for this it's essential to have a team and to speak with only one voice," Costa said. European leaders have been concerned that a U.S.-backed process will leave them sidelined and Kyiv vulnerable as Moscow and Washington decide the fate of a conflict that has roiled the continent. Ukraine is eager for support from its European allies. It's reluctant to leave the talks solely in the hands of a U.S. administration that has often seemed to lean toward Moscow's views. Russia does not want European countries involved in direct negotiations, complaining they are financing and supplying Ukraine's military effort. European leaders also distrust U.S. President Donald Trump to negotiate on their behalf after a series of tense standoffs over trade, Greenland and conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. "Without Europeans, there is no support for Ukraine," French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday at a meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin. "There is no more U.S. support." "At the end of the day, we will be the ones to define and decide for our future security as Europeans," he said. European leaders fear Russian President Vladimir Putin will press Trump to back a peace settlement that weakens not just Ukraine but broader European security. Putin has demanded NATO troops be pulled back from Russia's borders and that no European forces be deployed in Ukraine. As envoys from Washington, Moscow and Kyiv met this week in Abu Dhabi, several European countries, including the U.K., France and Germany, attended discussions nearby, but not the main talks. U.S. envoy Jared Kushner and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said after they met in Dublin late Thursday that Europe would be part of the next round of talks. Zelenskyy said Europe would send a negotiating team, adding, "They will have a voice." "We cannot conclude this deal without the Europeans being at the table," Kushner said. He said Putin "is willing to give it a try." European leaders are united in wanting a place at the table. But they have tussled over whether Europe should be represented by one person — as Russia has demanded and the U.S. suggested it would prefer — or a team. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Thursday that "the Europeans squabble like spiders in a jar" and they should name a representative. Supporters of a single envoy, such as Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, argued that the absence of a united European voice has allowed individual countries or small groups to engage in freelance diplomacy. "There are too many different groupings discussing the issue," she said. The question of who represents Europe is an old one. Europe itself is loosely defined. Is it the 27-nation EU, the 32-nation NATO military alliance made up mostly of European countries, the 29-nation Schengen zone, or the 47-nation European Political Community? After this week's U.S.-brokered talks between Ukraine and Russia in the United Arab Emirates, Kushner said that "if Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation." That echoes the famous question often misattributed to former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger: "Who do I call if I want to call Europe?" The decision to send a team, rather than an individual, allows for participation by members of the "coalition of the willing," a group of nations that have pledged to underpin a future ceasefire with military support. That includes the U.K., which left the EU in 2020. Poland is a voice for nations on the EU's eastern flank that face constant hybrid threats from Russia, including influence campaigns and disruptive drones. It was not immediately clear who would represent the EU's institutions. Speculation had centered on Costa and the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas. Earlier this year, Costa faced criticism within the EU after his office set up a hush-hush back-channel with Moscow. Kallas, a former prime minister of Estonia, laid claim to the envoy role Friday, saying, "I'm the one who is representing Europe in the foreign and security policy." "I know that the Russians don't want me, but, you know, do we have a say, who is representing Russia?" she said. "We can't send any person that has no institutional role like the Americans are sending." "In my opinion, calling them negotiations is an exaggeration," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Thursday. "We will not build a new security architecture simply because the Russian president, or someone in the United States, wishes it." With Trump due to head to Beijing next week to meet Putin, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said European leaders feared another "Anchorage moment," a reference to the Alaska summit where they were stunned by Trump's overtures to the Russian leader in the absence of Ukrainian or European envoys. "Please, no surprises," Merz said. "Continue to play in team Europe and in the team with Ukraine." Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs noted that Europe is larger than Russia in population, economy and military might. Associated Press writers Geir Moulson in Berlin, Lorne Cook in Brussels and Colleen Barry in Milan contributed to this report.

Dollars Rain From Balcony As Kazakhstan's State Giants Rocked By Corruption Arrests
articles.summary: Days after security services detained the heads of Samruk-Kazyna and state railway KTZ, which control 40 percent of Kazakhstan’s economy, President Toqaev convened an urgent Security Council meeting to reinforce his “Law and Order” drive, address transport governance, and reassure foreign investors.
articles.body: Bundles of greenbacks tumbled from a balcony in an upscale residential complex in the Kazakh capital as two titans of the country's economy were shaken by the arrests of their bosses on corruption charges. The following day, Kazakh President Qasym-Zhomart Toqaev called an extraordinary meeting of his Security Council and declared corruption to be the "Achilles heel" of state-owned companies. The events of November 12-13 have made for a busy news cycle in Kazakhstan, even if the details remain murky. There's no clear link between the dollar downpour and the arrests, but more on that later. The people arrested on November 12 are major figures leading two of Kazakhstan's most powerful state-owned institutions. Nurlan Zhakupov is chairman of Samruk-Kazyna, the country's sovereign wealth fund. In its 2021 annual report , the state-owned fund said it controlled "almost all strategic assets" of Kazakhstan's corporate sector, representing nearly 40 percent of GDP. Its total assets reached approximately $87.5 billion at the end of 2025. Yelzhas Otynshiyev is head of Kazakhstan Temir Zholy (KTZ), the state-run rail operator, which has been preparing for an IPO of up to 20 percent of its shares on the London, Hong Kong, and Kazakh stock exchanges, with a potential valuation of up to $5 billion, according to a Samruk-Kazyna press release . Both men were appointed to senior roles during Toqaev's presidency after successful careers in major Western companies. Toqaev described the arrests as "an extremely serious signal of widespread corruption in state-owned companies" and said they should be seen as part of a broader effort to ensure equality before the law following constitutional changes he rammed through earlier this year. Critics have said the changes are more about cementing his grip on power than anything else. They were followed by an election in August , roundly criticized by international observers, in which a new political party dedicated to pushing Toqaev's political agenda won 70 percent of the vote. Speaking on November 13, Toqaev focused on hard-hitting anti-corruption rhetoric. He cited more than 3,100 corruption offenses identified between 2023 and 2025, involving some $560 million, and insisted that no official, regardless of position or connections, should be above the law. "There will, of course, be no distinction between 'our own', 'not quite our own' and, even more so, 'outsiders'. Our constitution enshrines the principle that all citizens are equal before the law. We must uphold this requirement," he said. Founded in 2008 under then-President Nursultan Nazarbayev, Samruk-Kazyna is also central to major state-backed deals with foreign companies and international lenders. Several of its subsidiaries, including uranium producer Kazatomprom, oil giant KazMunayGas, and airline Air Astana, have already been listed on stock exchanges. KTZ's IPO was expected to fund Kazakhstan's railway modernization and expand capacity across the vast country, including along the Trans-Caspian corridor linking China and Europe. It remains unclear whether the listing will go ahead as planned. Rubio Heads To Central Asia As US Seeks Bigger Role In Region Dominated By Russia, China Financial analyst Rasul Rysmambetov told RFE/RL that some potential investors were taking news of the arrests calmly, provided the company's accounts remained reliable. "KTZ's IPO can and should be postponed, though more for financial reasons than reputational ones," Rysmambetov said. "If it turns out this was a bribe rather than money stolen directly from projects, investors will take it fairly neutrally. Those who have already invested in Kazakhstan say: 'The main thing is that the financial reports aren't fabricated.'" Toqaev said some agreements and contracts had recently been reviewed because, in his view, they had been signed erroneously. He gave no details and did not link them to the current investigation. Political analyst Dosym Satpayev says Samruk-Kazyna and much of Kazakhstan's wider quasi-public sector have long operated like a "black box." He argues that replacing executives will not fix the underlying problems. "To paraphrase the plumber from an old joke: It's not just the tap that needs fixing here -- the entire system at the fund needs to be changed!" he wrote, questioning why Samruk-Kazyna had failed to become the kind of state investment institution originally envisioned, modeled on Singapore's Temasek Holdings state-owned global investment firm. Economist Olzhas Khudaibergenov, a former economic adviser to Toqaev, sees the KTZ arrests as an opportunity to confront entrenched corruption. He described the alleged networks inside the railway operator in stark terms: "There are legends that an entire mafia operates there, capable of sabotaging orders and even derailing a passenger train so that an honest manager is dismissed in the scandal that follows." The Horrors Of Aktas Mental Hospital: Inside Kazakhstan's Secretive Asylum He questioned whether detaining three or four executives would be enough to dismantle such networks and whether anyone would be willing to take on the backlash involved in cleaning up the company. The arrests have also reignited debate over whether Samruk-Kazyna should be reformed or broken up. Toqaev has offered no specific plan but has ordered the government and oversight agencies to submit proposals by November 24 to reduce corruption and improve the performance of quasi-public-sector companies. The same day that Kazakhstan's National Security Committee (KNB) announced the arrests, footage began circulating online that appeared to show suitcases and bundles of cash scattered outside the upscale Atlant residential complex in central Astana. The video shows uniformed police officers in high-visibility vests cordoning off the area alongside plainclothes officials. The building is close to the headquarters of both KTZ and Samruk-Kazyna. Authorities have not confirmed whether the incident is connected to the arrests or whether the bank notes are authentic. Some bloggers claimed one of the detained officials lived in the building and that eight suitcases and duffel bags filled with $100 bills had been thrown from a balcony as KNB officers arrived. Local media and online commentators have speculated that the cash amounted to between $15 million and $40 million, though no official figure has been released. The KNB did not respond to an inquiry from RFE/RL about whether the incident was linked to the arrests, how much cash was involved, or what has happened to the money. RFE/RL's Kazakh Service offers informed and accurate reporting in the Kazakh and Russian languages about issues that matter in Kazakhstan, while providing a dynamic platform for audience engagement and the free exchange of news and ideas.

Russia sends major business delegation to Kabul for business talks with the Taliban
articles.summary: A Russian deputy prime minister led a 70-strong Russian delegation to Afghanistan, pursuing deals on transport, logistics, agriculture, and health products with the Taliban.
articles.body: Russian deputy prime minister Alexei Overchuk was welcomed by a guard of honour when he arrived in Kabul on Thursday with a delegation of 70 Russian business people to conduct business talks with the Taliban government, Afghan officials said.Overchuk met Taliban prime minister Mohammad Hassan Akhund, the deputy prime minister for economic affairs Abdul Ghani Baradar as well as foreign minister Amir Khan Muttaqi.According to a statement by the Afghan government published on X, Abdul Ghani Baradar described to the Russians Afghanistan's potential for economic development and investment, pointing to "strategic location, abundant resources and a workforce of 24 million people".Abdul Ghani Baradar invited Russian companies to invest in agriculture, mining, constructions of roads, railways and factories, and to create a special economic zone in Afghanistan, while expressing his wish to expand exports of Afghan agricultural products to Russia.The deputy prime minister also asked Russia to "provide the necessary facilities for Afghan products to be supplied to Russian markets and to cooperate in reducing transport and transit costs".A Russian news agency quoted Alexei Overchuk as saying that the Russian delegation represent companies that are already operating in Afghanistan and that "many others want to start operating in this country."Overchuk said that the companies represented in the delegation work in the fields of transport, logistics, agriculture and pharmaceuticals and that the Afghan government is interested in Russian chemical fertilisers, as well as in "building fertiliser production plants on Afghan soil".Overchuk estimated that trade between Russia and Afghanistan in the first eight months of 2026 had more than doubled, reaching over 349 million dollars.Russia officially recognised the Taliban government in July 2025, being the only state to have taken such a step since the Taliban seized power in August 2021, after the withdrawal of the United States.Although no country other than Russia has formally recognised the new Afghan regime, the Taliban authorities have so far held high-level talks with many states and have established specific diplomatic and economic relations with some governments.

articles.title: Bahrain Says It Intercepted Iranian Attacks As Tehran Claims Strike On US Base
articles.summary: Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks on November 15, after explosions and air raid sirens were reported across the Gulf kingdom and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed it had targeted a US military installation.
articles.body: Bahrain said its air defenses intercepted and destroyed several Iranian aerial attacks on November 15, after explosions and air raid sirens were reported across the Gulf kingdom and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed it had targeted a US military installation. The Bahraini military said its air defenses intercepted several attacks before they reached their targets, accusing Tehran of continuing its "systematic hostile approach" toward the kingdom. Bahrain's Foreign Ministry said the country rejected "turning its territory into an arena for settling scores" and held Iran fully responsible for the attacks and their consequences. Iran's IRGC claimed they had launched six drones targeting a US air defense radar system at the Al-Riffa helicopter base in Bahrain, according to statements carried by Iranian state media. There was no immediate confirmation from US or Bahraini authorities that the radar installation had been hit. Citing its journalists in Bahrain, the AFP news agency reported that explosions were heard around 4 a.m. local time, followed by another series of blasts around 6:30 a.m. Sirens also sounded and Bahraini authorities issued warnings urging residents to seek shelter without specifying the source of the threat. The Interior Ministry told residents to remain calm, proceed to the nearest safe location, and follow official channels for updates. Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, has been among the Gulf countries targeted by Iran during the conflict, which began on February 28 with US and Israeli strikes on Iran. The reported attack on November 15 came two days after the IRGC said it had targeted a US early-warning radar facility in Bahrain. The US military said at the time that it had intercepted two Iranian drones targeting the island, reporting no casualties or damage. Bahrain has now been targeted twice in three days, following a lull in attacks. The latest developments come amid diplomatic efforts to end the nearly nine-month conflict, which have not yet produced a breakthrough despite a broader lull in fighting. Iran has restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key global oil transit route, and launched missile and drone attacks on military and civilian infrastructure across the region. US President Donald Trump has told his senior advisers in recent days that he might refrain from further attacks on Iran if Tehran and Iran-backed Houthi fighters in Yemen avoid new provocations, according to Reuters. Trump has also said the US naval blockade of Iran would remain in place. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's military said on November 15 it had intercepted two Houthi ballistic missiles launched toward Riyadh and three drones in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province. RFE/RL journalists report the news in 24 languages in 18 countries where a free press is banned by the government or not fully established. We provide what many people cannot get locally: uncensored news, responsible discussion, and open debate.

articles.title: US denies IRGC destroyed American radar in Bahrain after attack on southern Iran
articles.summary: Despite rising military tensions, diplomatic efforts mediated by Qatar and Pakistan are continuing. Tehran has made any resumption of formal negotiations with Washington conditional on its demands being met.
articles.body: The US has rejected claims by Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that its forces destroyed an American early-warning radar in Bahrain.US Central Command (CENTCOM) said on Friday that the IRGC had launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and that both had been shot down by US forces."There were no injuries or damage," it said.The Guard's aerospace force fighters had reportedly launched a strike in response to an attack on a telecommunications tower in Sirik County in southern Iran on Thursday.The IRGC said in a statement that the strike was a "serious warning" to Washington "to put an end to its aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz," per the Fars news agency.It added that its forces were on "full alert and ready to respond without geographical limits" should "such violations and acts of aggression" happen again.Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet, which plays an important role in maintaining Washington’s naval operations in the Persian Gulf and surrounding waters.CENTCOM said on Wednesday that American forces were continuing to "work around the clock keeping the Strait of Hormuz open for commercial shipping" while also "strictly enforcing the ironclad naval blockade against Iran."According to CENTCOM, around 1.7 billion barrels of crude oil have passed through the strategic strait under US protection since the summer.The latest confrontation comes as US President Donald Trump has taken an increasingly hard line against Iran.Trump said on Thursday that Washington no longer needed an agreement with Iran and asked Vice President JD Vance, who had played a role in diplomatic efforts, to focus on domestic issues at home.Trump also said that Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain had asked him to postpone broader attacks against the country.Despite rising military tensions, diplomatic efforts mediated by Qatar and Pakistan are continuing. Tehran has made any resumption of formal negotiations with Washington conditional on its demands being met, including the lifting of sanctions, an end to the naval blockade of Iranian ports, the release of frozen assets and a halt to the war on all fronts.

articles.title: Russia's Propaganda Machine Deploys Pro-War AI Songs
articles.summary: Russians using streaming music sites might find a new genre turning up in their feeds: AI-generated songs in support of Russia's military and the war in Ukraine. A study by a Ukrainian nonprofit, Terrecon, found nearly 1,000 songs in that category, and researchers say they are meant to generate patriotic sentiment, help mobilize new recruits, and even appeal to children.
articles.body: Russians using streaming music sites might find a new genre turning up in their feeds: AI-generated songs in support of Russia's military and the war in Ukraine. A study by a Ukrainian nonprofit, Terrecon, found nearly 1,000 songs in that category aimed at generating patriotic sentiment.

articles.title: Australian MP 'full of gratitude' upon leaving hospital after alleged car attack
articles.summary: The MP lost both of her legs after the alleged attack outside her electorate office four weeks ago.
articles.body: Independent MP Helen Haines has been released from hospital after an alleged attack last month Australian politician Helen Haines has said she is "full of gratitude" upon being discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked with a car and left a double amputee. The independent MP was struck outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on October 19, an incident which horrified Australia. Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a public official. He has yet to enter pleas. In her first public comments since the attack, Haines, 65, said she had moved into the rehabilitation stage of her recovery. "This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage," Haines said. "I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing." She added that she had been "overwhelmed" by the generosity of well wishers who had donated to Save the Children in her honour. Haines, known for supporting stronger climate action and helping establish a national anti-corruption commission, entered parliament in 2019 as the Member for Indi after working as a nurse and midwife. Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established. Nugent's father said he and his wife had been long-time friends of Haines, and Nugent's lawyer has said his client has mental health concerns. The incident sparked a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of public debate. Though a motive is still unclear, politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said he had been in regular contact with Haines and her "extraordinary" family. "All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery," he said in a statement. "We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation." 'Targeted' attack on much-loved MP leaves Australian town heartbroken

Russian envoy outlines Moscow’s concerns over Switzerland’s OSCE chairmanship
articles.summary: He noted that the Russian and Swiss delegations meet every week and that the Swiss side does not withhold information from Russia, Dmitry Polyansky said
articles.body: VIENNA, November 15. /TASS/. Switzerland maintained regular diplomatic contacts with Russia during its chairmanship of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), but generally sided with the European Union on key issues, Russia’s Permanent Representative to the OSCE Dmitry Polyansky told TASS. "I have no complaints about the Swiss when it comes to maintaining diplomatic contacts," Polyansky said. He noted that the Russian and Swiss delegations meet every week and that the Swiss side does not withhold information from Russia. However, the envoy described Switzerland’s neutrality as highly conditional, saying that Bern follows an openly pro-Ukrainian policy, even if it cannot be described as explicitly anti-Russian. "I cannot say that our voice goes unheard at the OSCE, that they prevent us from speaking or otherwise restrict us. But when they have to make a choice, they, of course, tend to take a position closer to that of the European Union rather than remain neutral. That is our main complaint," Polyansky said. As an example, Polyansky cited the Swiss chairmanship’s refusal to change the wording of a standing agenda item at OSCE meetings, which describes Russia’s special military operation as military aggression against Ukraine. He said this wording prevents Moscow from fully presenting its position. "They had the authority to make that decision and promised to consider changing the wording. But they ultimately decided that making such a change would send the wrong signal to Russia and suggest that they were abandoning their policy of solidarity with Brussels," the Russian envoy said. "How should we interpret this? Could they have changed it? Of course. Did they want to? Clearly, they did not.".

articles.title: The Constitutional Court will resume hearings tomorrow on Georgian Dream’s lawsuit seeking to ban five opposition parties
articles.summary: The Constitutional Court will resume hearings on November 16 regarding Georgian Dream’s lawsuit seeking to ban five opposition political parties. For reference, proceedings on the lawsuit began at the Constitutional Court on October 21.
articles.body: The Constitutional Court will resume hearings on November 16 regarding Georgian Dream’s lawsuit seeking to ban five opposition political parties. For reference, proceedings on the lawsuit began at the Constitutional Court on October 21. The case is being heard by the Plenum of the Constitutional Court, consisting of seven judges. The lawsuit submitted to the Constitutional Court is signed by 88 members of parliament. Based on their petition, the Court is considering declaring the following five political parties unconstitutional: The constitutional lawsuit is accompanied by the findings of the temporary investigative commission established in the 11th convocation of Parliament.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: US proposes Kyiv cede land to Russia for Nato membership, Zelenskyy says
articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has asked for the first time if Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the eastern Donbas region that Russia does not control in exchange for Ukraine becoming a Nato member . But the Ukrainian president said his country would not surrender territory.
articles.body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the US has asked for the first time if Ukraine would withdraw from parts of the eastern Donbas region that Russia does not control in exchange for Ukraine becoming a Nato member . But the Ukrainian president said his country would not surrender territory. “The Americans raised a question: ‘What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?’,” he said in remarks to reporters released by his office on Saturday. “That is why ⁠I believe Nato is back on the agenda.” But he said the suggestion, which would form part of a new postwar security framework for Europe, could allow Russia to weaken Nato and reshape borders. “This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said. Zelenskyy reiterated his position that Kyiv was not ready to concede territory but said that if it received a comprehensive package including security guarantees, the right to a strong and well-funded ​Ukrainian army and funds to rebuild, he would put the question to a ‌national referendum. Echoing comments ‌made by European leaders at a summit in Dublin on Friday, Zelenskyy dismissed Russia’s call for a broad agreement on European security architecture to be reached before the specifics are ‌agreed on how to end the war in Ukraine. “We cannot turn everything upside down and start by talking about changing the security framework in the world or across the continent overall, and only then talk about ending this war. This war must be ended first,” he said. The Ukrainian president has also rejected the possibility of Ukraine committing to neutrality , something that could only happen if the country’s constitution was changed. “If Putin expects Ukraine’s neutrality to be enshrined, that’s not going to happen,” he said. “We’re not in Nato right now anyway.” US President ⁠Donald Trump’s ⁠envoy and ​son-in-law Jared ⁠Kushner said on ⁠Saturday ​the US ‌was ‌focused on ‌facilitating direct engagement between Russia and ‌European nations on ​the Ukraine war , ⁠after trilateral meetings ​involving Washington, ​Moscow ​and ​Kyiv ‌this ​week. However, Washington and Nato have not yet commented on the suggestion of a swap of the Donbas for Ukraine Nato membership. Negotiations did, however, lead to agreements that European countries would join future talks on ending the war. Zelenskyy has accused SpaceX of not telling the truth over restrictions to Ukraine’s Starshield satellite system , saying the decision to impose speed limits appears to be “political” rather than “technical”. Speaking on Friday, Ukraine’s president said the restrictions affecting Ukrainian drones, in place for five days, meant they could no longer intercept incoming jet-powered Russian Shahed drones. Ukraine suspects the slowdown is a deliberate US tactic, designed to put pressure on Zelenskyy to make concessions to Putin. French President Emmanuel Macron said Saturday that countries seeking to limit aid to Ukraine want to impose an “unjust peace” and warned that it was a recipe for another war . “Those who want to ration aid to Ukraine wish underneath it all to force an unjust peace on it” and, by extension, all of Europe, Macron said on social media. “That is a recipe for another war. That cannot be France’s position.” Russian forces ⁠struck a cargo vessel in ⁠the ⁠Ukrainian ​port of Chornomorsk , RIA ⁠news agency cited the Russian ⁠defence ministry ​as ‌saying on ‌Saturday. The ministry ‌said the ship was being used to supply the Ukrainian ‌military. Meanwhile, Ukrainian strikes on the Samara oil pipeline station near the village of Prosvet in Russia’s Samara region on Friday set several oil storage tanks on fire, Ukraine’s General Staff said. The facility is a key part of the network exporting Russian oil to global markets, the General Staff said. Separately, 22 people were injured in a Russian attack on the south-east Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia on Friday, Ukraine’s Emergency Service said.

articles.title: Nikoloski: respect for the Constitutional Court shows institutional maturity
articles.summary: As a Government, we are making every effort to establish a functional system of the rule of law as the foundation of a democratic state, and here, of course, one of the key actors is the Constitutional Court, which has a special and irreplaceable role in preserving the constitutional order and protecting fundamental rights and freedoms, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Transport Aleksandar Nikoloski…
articles.body: As a Government, we are making every effort to establish a functional system of the rule of law as the foundation of a democratic state, and here, of course, one of the key actors is the Constitutional Court, which has a special and irreplaceable role in preserving the constitutional order and protecting fundamental rights and freedoms, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Transport Aleksandar Nikoloski said in his address at the fourth annual conference of the Forum of Balkan Constitutional Courts, held in Ohrid on the topic “Contemporary Challenges to the Rule of Law: The Role of Constitutional Courts.” Nikoloski stressed that the role of the Constitutional Court is particularly important in this time of rapid social, technological, and political changes. As he put it, “that is why institutions must be stable, institutions must be resilient, and institutions must survive political changes.” The independence, professionalism, and integrity of constitutional judges and of the Constitutional Court are key to fulfilling this function. The rule of law implies not only the adoption of high-quality decisions, but also their respect and implementation. The executive and legislative branches have the responsibility to create the conditions for the full implementation of the decisions of the Constitutional Court, which very often also mean a correction of certain decisions that may have been taken without sufficient analysis and without sufficiently taking all the facts into account, and sometimes even with some other intention. That is why the foundation of the Constitutional Court is precisely this — to help make corrections where corrections need to be made, Nikoloski pointed out. He noted that respect for constitutional justice is an indicator of a state’s institutional maturity and democratic responsibility. That is why we strive to respect the Constitutional Court and to give it the place it deserves in the state-legal order. The independence of the judiciary should, of course, not be understood in isolation from the other institutions, but rather as a guarantee of impartial and objective decision-making, and also as a way of improving society. Mutual control and balance among the three branches of power — and here, of course, the Constitutional Court as a separate body — play a significant role in maintaining a functional state, Nikoloski emphasized in his address before constitutional judges from the country and abroad. The Deputy Prime Minister also referred to the new challenges, such as digitalization and artificial intelligence, which on the one hand can be an advantage, but on the other hand also a threat. Of course, knowledge, experience, and the human factor remain irreplaceable, and I cannot agree with certain debates that are being conducted, that even in this area — in the area of respecting the Constitution, in the area of implementing the Constitution, and in the area of implementing and respecting the laws — we should rely on artificial intelligence. I think that is wrong, and I think it is something that we need to think about very seriously as a state and as states, because this is a broader debate, not only in our country, but I repeat, I believe that is not the path we should follow, because knowledge and personal experience are something that is irreplaceable and that no machine can do, Nikoloski said. At the closing of the Forum of Balkan Constitutional Courts, Deputy Prime Minister Nikoloski stressed that a strong state does not mean only a strong executive power, but a limited executive power, a state with strong and independent institutions, institutions that complement each other and control one another. Therefore, as a representative of the executive branch, as Deputy Prime Minister, I can say that as a Government we will do everything and we are doing everything for this system to continue to function and to be further developed, Nikoloski said.

articles.title: Appeals Court Lifts House Arrest on Klevi Metaj, Student Symbol of Albania’s Protests, as Police Keep Issuing On-the-Spot Fines
articles.summary: Tirana’s Court of Appeals on Friday lifted the house arrest imposed on Klevi Metaj, the 22-year-old law student who became the face of Albania’s student protests after footage showed him clashing with police officers and later handcuffed to the railings of the Ministry of Education.
articles.body: Tirana’s Court of Appeals on Friday lifted the house arrest imposed on Klevi Metaj, the 22-year-old law student who became the face of Albania’s student protests after footage showed him clashing with police officers and later handcuffed to the railings of the Ministry of Education. The court replaced house arrest with an obligation to report once a month to the relevant authority, according to Metaj’s lawyers. They had appealed the earlier decision of the Tirana court of first instance, which ordered house arrest after he was detained at the Oct. 13 protest . The lawyers said a criminal complaint has also been registered against the police officers involved, over what they describe as degrading and inhuman treatment of Metaj during his detention. Metaj, a University of Tirana student, became widely known on Oct. 13, when students clashed with police outside the Education Ministry. Photos showed him handcuffed to the ministry’s fence, and other images showed him with visible injuries inside a police van. He was taken to a hospital, where he was handcuffed to his bed. The Tirana court then ordered house arrest. On Friday, the Court of Appeals lifted that measure. The ruling comes as police continue to fine protesters on the spot under two emergency acts the government adopted in late October . Since the acts took effect, police have fined protesters 5,000 lek (about €55 or $62) each, mainly for blocking roads or standing peacefully on the boulevard. Partial police figures show more than 65 people fined. Media outlets and civil society groups count more than 100 , and they say the real number is likely higher because not all fines are reported. Unlike Metaj, those fined have not been brought before a judge. Lawyers and rights groups say the fines are imposed at the scene, without a court review or an individual assessment of what each person did. The government’s package also includes measures that give police the right to restrict protests near institutions, remove people from designated “protected zones” and fine participants. Fines can reach 500,000 lek (about €5,500 or $6,200). Last week, student groups asked the Constitutional Court to strike down the acts and to suspend them until it rules on their constitutionality. The protests began on May 31 over a tourism project in the protected Zvernec area on the southern coast. They grew into a broader movement against corruption and the rising cost of living, and in October students clashed with police in Tirana. Protesters are demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama.

articles.title: Constitutional Court rejects UNM motion to recuse judge Eva Gotsiridze
articles.summary: The Plenum of Georgia's Constitutional Court has rejected a motion filed by the United National Movement (UNM) seeking the recusal of Judge Eva Gotsiridze. The decision was announced by Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraya.
articles.body: The Plenum of Georgia's Constitutional Court has rejected a motion filed by the United National Movement (UNM) seeking the recusal of Judge Eva Gotsiridze. The decision was announced by Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraya. "The Plenum rejects the motion as unfounded," Nadaraya said. He explained that the main argument raised by the UNM concerned the wording of questions asked by Gotsiridze, which the party claimed suggested that she had already formed an opinion on the case. Nadaraya referred to one of the judge's questions: "Does the party not share responsibility?" He said the question was intended to establish the party's position on whether it accepted any responsibility and did not indicate that the judge had prejudged the case. "The formulation of this question does not express any preconceived opinion or indicate that a position has already been formed," Nadaraya said. He added that the Plenum's members had unanimously concluded that the motion appeared to be an attempt to prevent the judge from asking critical questions necessary for an objective decision. "The court is obliged to ask questions about all the allegations raised and hear the parties' views on them," he said. Nadaraya also stressed that even sharply worded questions did not mean that a judge had already taken a position in favor of either party. Earlier, representatives of the United National Movement asked the Constitutional Court to recuse Gotsiridze from the proceedings. The party's representative, Ana Tsitlidze, said the motion was based on the combination of the judge's comments during the hearing and her reaction to the respondent's answers. "These circumstances give an objective observer reasonable grounds to doubt that the judge has already formed a negative attitude toward the central issue in the dispute," Tsitlidze said. Georgia’s Constitutional Court is continuing to hear a high-stakes lawsuit seeking to ban five opposition parties, with this week’s proceedings marked by disputes over evidence, procedural rights and the timing of any potential ruling. Tensions inside the courtroom have also escalated, with two leading representatives of the Coalition for Change ordered to leave Wednesday’s hearing. The case, brought by 88 members of the ruling Georgian Dream party, seeks to have five political groups declared unconstitutional and prohibited from operating: United National Movement; Coalition for Change, comprising Gvaramia, Melia, Girchi and Droa; Strong Georgia–Lelo, For the People, For Freedom!; the Federalist Party; and Gakharia Tor Georgia. The petition argues that the parties’ activities threaten Georgia’s constitutional order, independence, and territorial integrity. It also draws on the findings of a temporary parliamentary investigative commission established during the 11th convocation of Parliament. The opposition parties reject the allegations, describing the case as politically motivated and warning that a ban would remove a substantial part of the country’s political opposition. The Constitutional Court began examining the petition on October 21. The case is being heard by a seven-judge plenary panel, and a final ruling is expected by June 2027. The decision will be final and cannot be appealed within Georgia.

The information was confirmed in a joint statement by the press services of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, the Prosecutor General's Office, and the Azerbaijan Mine Action Agency (ANAMA). According to the information, the explosion occurred as a result of Rasul Shahin oglu Ibrahimov, born in 1986 and a resident of Demirchilar village in the Gazakh district, and Sahib Amrahov, born in 1982 and a resident of Dash Salahli village in the Gazakh district, handling unexploded ordnance. articles.body: The ALDE Party has adopted a resolution titled "Protecting Political Pluralism and Ending Political Repression in Georgia." Through this document, ALDE calls on the Georgian authorities to "end the ban on opposition parties, release political prisoners, and call new elections." "We condemn: 'Georgian Dream's' authoritarian repressions, including court proceedings aimed at banning parties, politically motivated persecution, penalties for online criticism, restrictions on civic space, and impunity for the abuse of force, all of which violate international standards. An end to the banning of opposition parties, including circumvention through successor parties, and political exclusion based on party affiliation or employment by foreign-funded organizations; political participation must be guaranteed. The immediate and unconditional release of political prisoners and those detained for exercising their fundamental rights. The dropping of politically motivated sabotage charges against opposition leaders, the protection of peaceful demonstrators, journalists, human rights defenders, and international organizations, and ensuring the monitoring of fair, independent court proceedings. An end to detentions and disproportionate fines for peaceful protests and expression, including online criticism; punitive provisions must be repealed. The repeal of repressive foreign agents and funding restrictions; the restoration of the ability for independent media, civil society, and human rights defenders to operate freely; the implementation of Venice Commission and OSCE recommendations; and independent investigations into torture, ill-treatment, and attacks. The holding of new, free, and fair parliamentary elections with impartial administration, international observation, unrestricted opposition participation, and protection against intimidation," the document states. The text of the resolution was distributed by the press service of the "Droa" party.

articles.title: Prosecutor’s Office charges former Penitentiary Service head Giorgi Pataridze and former Gldani prison director Ramaz Pirtskhalava over attack on Davit Peikrishvili
articles.summary: The Prosecutor's Office has charged former head of the Special Penitentiary Service Giorgi Pataridze and former director of Penitentiary Facility No. 8 Ramaz Pirtskhalava in connection with the attack on Davit Peikrishvili, who is linked to criminal circles, inside his prison cell. Pataridze is accused of exceeding his official powers, while Pirtskhalava faces charges of abuse of official powers.
articles.body: The Prosecutor's Office has charged former head of the Special Penitentiary Service Giorgi Pataridze and former director of Penitentiary Facility No. 8 Ramaz Pirtskhalava in connection with the attack on Davit Peikrishvili, who is linked to criminal circles, inside his prison cell. Pataridze is accused of exceeding his official powers, while Pirtskhalava faces charges of abuse of official powers. The announcement was made at a briefing held at the Prosecutor's Office just minutes ago. On October 16, 2026, Vato Kipiani, Shota Kipiani and Avtandil Bilanishvili, who had been arrested in connection with the same criminal case, were transferred to Penitentiary Facility No. 8. Before they were assigned to cells, at Vato Kipiani's request and on the instructions of Giorgi Pataridze, then head of the Special Penitentiary Service, the facility's director, Ramaz Pirtskhalava, decided to place the three men, together with Davit Kacharava, who was also being held at the facility, and convicted prisoner Pavle Gotsiridze, in Davit Peikrishvili's cell. The decision was made in gross violation of the requirements of Georgia's Penitentiary Code and the regulations governing Penitentiary Facility No. 8, the Prosecutor's Office said. On the same day, Vato Kipiani, Shota Kipiani, Avtandil Bilanishvili, Davit Kacharava and Pavle Gotsiridze allegedly physically assaulted Davit Peikrishvili as a group. The violence continued until October 20, 2026. As a result of the assault, Peikrishvili sustained multiple injuries across his body, including four fractured ribs, fractures of the transverse processes of his vertebrae and a concussion. His injuries were classified as less serious bodily harm resulting in a prolonged health disorder. Based on the evidence collected in the criminal investigation, former head of the Special Penitentiary Service Giorgi Pataridze was charged with exceeding his official powers, while former director of Penitentiary Facility No. 8 Ramaz Pirtskhalava was charged with abuse of official powers. Both offenses carry a prison sentence of up to three years. Related Story: Seven charged after Prosecutor’s Office confirms Davit Peikrishvili was beaten at Gldani prison

articles.summary: Russia’s state corporation Rosatom is set to begin construction of Kazakhstan’s first nuclear power plant (NPP) on the shores of Lake Balkhash, near the village of Ulken in the Almaty region, in 2027, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Agency for Atomic Energy Almassadam Satkaliyev said. «As you know, during the state visit of Russian President Vladimir Putin ...
articles.body: Russia’s state corporation Rosatom is set to begin construction of Kazakhstan’s first nuclear power plant (NPP) on the shores of Lake Balkhash, near the village of Ulken in the Almaty region, in 2027, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Agency for Atomic Energy Almassadam Satkaliyev said. «As you know, during the state visit of Russian President Vladimir Putin to Kazakhstan this spring, Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev announced that construction could begin in 2027… If all the requirements under Kazakhstan’s legislation are met, we understand that Rosatom, together with Kazakhstani partners, namely Kazakhstani companies, could begin construction in 2027. This is the scenario we envisage,» he told reporters on the sidelines of World Atomic Days in Antalya, Turkey. According to him, cooperation between Rosatom, Kazakhstan Nuclear Power Plants (KNPP), the government and the Agency for Atomic Energy has been fairly successful over the past period. «We have already signed an intergovernmental agreement with Russia this year. An EPC contract has also been signed, and fairly constructive negotiations are currently underway on all the necessary annexes. Overall, this lays the groundwork for beginning construction of the nuclear power plant in the near future,» Satkaliyev said. He noted that Rosatom has unique experience in implementing international projects. According to Rosatom CEO Alexey Likhachev, the state corporation is currently involved in the construction of 28 reactors outside Russia. The first 2.4-gigawatt nuclear power plant is expected to cost $15 billion and is scheduled to be commissioned in 2035. China’s CNNC will build two nuclear power plants of similar capacity. The first of these will be located near the village of Ulken, close to Rosatom’s plant.

Boxer on death row in Iran vows ‘not to bow before oppression’ after winning rights prize
articles.summary: Political prisoner Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran, given prestigious Magnitsky humanitarian award A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”.
articles.body: A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”. Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani , an Iranian boxing champion, coach and political prisoner, has been sentenced to death three times and is one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran . He was given the Magnitsky award for outstanding human rights activist at a ceremony in London on Thursday night. In a written message from Vakilabad prison in north-eastern Iran, he said: “I accept this award in the name of all those who, for the ‘crime’ of aspiring to a free Iran, have been imprisoned, tortured, threatened, or sentenced to death; in the name of my comrades in the resistance units and the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives.” He added: “The regime demands repentance, televised confessions and surrender from us. But our answer is clear: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’” Vafaei Sani, 31, was arrested in 2020 for taking part in nationwide democracy protests in 2019 and accused of supporting an opposition group, the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK). He was convicted of “corruption on Earth” and sentenced to death for a third time in September 2024 after “a grossly unfair trial”, according to Amnesty International. The supreme court upheld his death sentence on 4 October 2025. Since his arrest he has been tortured and held in solitary confinement for extended periods. His continued imprisonment has drawn widespread international condemnation from prominent sportspeople, human rights organisations and legal experts who have called for his immediate release and the annulment of his death sentence. The Magnitsky awards are named after the Russian lawyer, Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody after exposing government corruption . They began in 2015 as a way to recognise journalists, politicians and activists in the field of human rights. Sir William Browder, head of the Magnitsky Justice Foundation and the chair of the awards committee, said Vafaei Sani’s case was emblematic of the plight of many Iranians who face execution for standing against the regime. “Most important, Mohammad Javad is still alive,” he said. “That is why this award matters. Every time the world pays attention, it becomes harder to kill him quietly.” According to the Hengaw Organisation for Human Rights, at least 710 people have been executed in Iran since the beginning of 2026, including 79 political and religious prisoners. In an October report, the organisation documented at least 106 death sentences against January protest detainees, 35 of whom had already been executed . In Vakilabad prison, where Vafaei Sani is detained, five people have been executed linked to the protests and 15 others are facing death sentences. Vafaei Sani’s award comes at a time when there are growing fears for imprisoned Iranian athletes, who are considered role models in the country. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, founder of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The situation is really dire … We have seven athletes at risk of execution now, including Vafaei Sani.” Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a mountaineer, was executed on 14 October after the anti-government protests. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, earlier that month, and the mixed martial arts fighter Gholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hanged in May. Abdollahkhani said people had been celebrating Vafaei Sani’s award. “Even people who don’t support his political view are supporting him to be heard,” she said. “I find it very inspiring that different political groups are coming together to say no to execution.” In his message, Vafaei Sani said he wanted “a free and democratic Iran … where the people vote freely, women and men are equal, there is no discrimination on the basis of ethnicity, religion or belief, and no one is imprisoned or executed for political opposition”. He added: “I remain steadfast in my pledge, and I will not bow before oppression until the people of Iran are free.”

articles.summary: Supermarket giant says no customer, team or supplier data compromised but recommends updating passwords as a precaution Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised.
articles.body: Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised. Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts. “Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident,” the company said in a statement to the stock exchange. “We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles’ systems. “Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online.” Coles apologised to its customers for any concerns they might have at “a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world”. “We have security measures in place to protect customer and supplier accounts and are continuing to closely monitor our system,” it said. “We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reuse the same password across multiple services.” Coles also warned customers to be cautious if they received unexpected emails or SMS messages purporting to be from the retailer, and not to click any links. In a separate and unrelated incident, Woolworths said it was aware of reports from customers who purchased compromised e-gift cards. The ABC first reported on Monday some customers had lost hundreds of dollars after buying the company’s Everyday WISH gift cards through its rewards website or app, only to find the sums loaded on to them had been spent by someone else. Some customers told the national broadcaster they had lost up to $500, with transactions showing up at stores in different states to where they purchased the cards. “We are aware of reports of an issue affecting a number of customer e-gift cards and are looking into the matter as a priority,” a Woolworths spokesperson said in a statement. “We recognise the concern this has caused affected customers and we apologise to customers impacted. We encourage any customer who notices a transaction they don’t recognise to contact our Gift Card Support team.” The company says it is working through all reported issues and will look into replacing affected e-gift cards.

articles.title: Iran says it targeted US military radar in Bahrain in retaliatory strike
articles.summary: First direct attack on US military installations for months was in response to US airstrike on communications tower Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s first direct attack on US military installations for months.
articles.body: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it has targeted and destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in response to a US airstrike on a communications tower in Sirik overlooking the strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s first direct attack on US military installations for months. “This is a serious warning to the aggressor enemy to end its aerial mischief and oil smuggling in the strait of Hormuz,” the IRGC said. “In the event of repeated violations and aggression, the IRGC aerospace force is on full alert to confront the enemy without constraint.” US Central Command denied that the radar system had been destroyed and said US forces had intercepted two Iranian drones headed for Bahrain . Donald Trump has said in a series of media interviews over the past 24 hours that he will attack Iran only if necessary, claiming that Gulf countries, such as Saudi Arabia, have urged him to hold back from planned large-scale military strikes. Trump said he had asked the vice-president, JD Vance, to end his interest in negotiating a new deal with Iran and instead focus on corruption and fraud in Democrat-run cities and states. Vance had been seen by the Iranians as the most trustworthy figure close to Trump, but they had rejected his request for a personal meeting with their negotiators to discuss the terms of a peace deal. Vance has been at the forefront of Republicans saying the war was the cause of the widespread Republican losses in the midterms. Trump said he had been disappointed in the American public because higher diesel prices were a small price to pay for preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. An opinion poll in the UK showed 65% of the British public would oppose the US resuming the war in Iran, and only 14% would back it. The poll was conducted by YouGov for the Council for Arab-British Understanding (Caabu). It also found 54% oppose UK bases being used by the US to mount attacks on Iran, with 29% in favour. Support for additional UK sanctions against Iran was 45%, with 22% opposed. The poll was conducted on Tuesday and Wednesday this week, before two Iranians were found guilty on Thursday of spying and planning attacks on journalists in the UK. The Iranian embassy has rejected the court judgment as an attempt to advance a political agenda. Chris Doyle, the director of Caabu, said: “The British public are sceptical about any war on Iran and what it might achieve. What might make the Burnham government take note is the very high level of opposition to any further war amongst 2024 Labour voters, at 79%.” Iran’s Assembly of Experts, a body of elected Islamic jurists responsible for choosing the supreme leader, has become the first governing institution in Iran to call for a review of the country’s defence doctrine, potentially leading to religious permission for Iran to try to acquire a nuclear weapon. In a statement released on Thursday, the assembly called for a review of Iran’s membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty, describing the move as an “unavoidable necessity” and a “public and national demand”. The intervention carries a religious as much as political significance because the 88-strong assembly comprises senior clerics, most of whom are supposed to be qualified to exercise independent Islamic legal reasoning. Iran has had a longstanding prohibition on nuclear weapons, based on a fatwa issued by the late supreme leader Ali Khamenei, but the relevance of the fatwa in the wake of the US attacks on Iran has been questioned widely in political and security circles. Whether Iran has the stockpiles of uranium or technology to build a nuclear weapon is contested. The UN nuclear inspectorate has expressed alarm about a continued lack of information from Iran about its nuclear sites. It said: “Our concerns are growing over Iran’s refusal to allow access to design information or inspections of the Isfahan facility. We do not know the exact location of the Isfahan uranium enrichment facility or whether it contains nuclear materials. It is imperative that we carry out our verification activities in Iran without further delay.”
